findings.claim: Surah 21:30 says: “The heavens and the earth were joined together, then We split them apart.”
findings.truth: No recognised translation reads that way. Abdel Haleem 21:30 has “the heavens and the earth used to be joined together and that We ripped them apart”; The Clear Quran has “the heavens and earth were once one mass then We split them apart”. The lesson blends the two and presents the result as a verbatim quotation. The reference 21:30 and the sense are right.

findings.claim: Q3 (4 marks): “Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about the origin of the universe.”
findings.truth: The spec names only three Theme B issues on which contrasting beliefs must be explained with reference to Christianity and one or more other religious traditions: abortion, euthanasia and animal experimentation. The origin of the universe is not one of them, so a contrasting-beliefs question is unlikely to be set on it. The content itself is examinable, so no edit.

findings.claim: This is one of the AQA “contrasting beliefs” topics
findings.truth: Student-facing text must never name the exam board.

findings.claim: Card 4 question begins with a stray closing quote mark: ” _____ Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) ...
findings.truth: Mangled generator output with a bare one-word answer. Reshaped as a Who... question answered “Pope Francis”.

findings.claim: Card 5: “The _____ of England has committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2030”, answer “Church”.
findings.truth: A single-word cloze with no question stem. Reshaped as a Which... question answered “The Church of England”. The 2030 net zero target is itself correct (General Synod endorsed the routemap in July 2022).
findings.evidence: churchofengland.org environment and climate change page

findings.claim: After 24 weeks, abortion is only permitted if the mother’s life is at risk or the foetus has a severe abnormality.
findings.truth: A third ground has no time limit: a risk of grave permanent injury to the woman’s physical or mental health. The omission is a simplification, not a claim that would cost marks.

findings.claim: There are different types: voluntary euthanasia ... non-voluntary euthanasia ... and assisted suicide (helping someone end their own life).
findings.truth: Assisted suicide is normally treated as distinct from euthanasia, not a type of it, because the person performs the final act. Lesson 4 gives the fuller active/passive split. Common GCSE shorthand, so no edit.
findings.evidence: Suicide Act 1961 s.2; standard GCSE RS usage

findings.claim: Card 4 answer (the ‘double effect’ definition) runs to 31 words.
findings.truth: The validator caps a flashcard answer at 30 words. Shortened to 28 words with the same meaning; the glossary entry keeps the fuller wording.

findings.claim: Lessons 3 and 4 carry almost the same title and cover the same spec content (abortion, euthanasia, sanctity and quality of life); lesson 3 also repeats lesson 5’s afterlife material.
findings.truth: Two builds sit in one unit. Lessons 4 and 5 are the older build (auto-generated “Cover this box” revision tips, generated diagrams). Lessons 1-3 are a newer build (hand-written tips, <!-- DIAGRAM --> placeholders). Options: (a) retire lesson 4 and trim the afterlife section out of lesson 3 so lesson 5 owns it; (b) keep lesson 4 and re-scope lesson 3 to sanctity and quality of life only; (c) keep both and rename lesson 4. Recommendation: (a). Lesson 3 is the better written of the pair and lesson 5 already covers the afterlife in full. Not edited.
findings.evidence: raw/L03.txt vs raw/L04.txt; revision-tip style and diagram state

findings.claim: Under the 1990 Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act, abortion is legal in the UK up to 24 weeks ...
findings.truth: The Act that legalises abortion is the Abortion Act 1967; the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 only amended it to set the 24-week limit. The 1967 Act does not extend to Northern Ireland, so the law described covers England, Scotland and Wales. Lesson 3 states this correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Abortion Act 1967 as amended by HFEA 1990 s.37; raw/L03.txt

findings.claim: A crush resulted in 97 deaths and left Tony in a persistent vegetative state
findings.truth: 94 people died on the day of the Hillsborough disaster (15 April 1989). The toll reached 97 only in 2021, and Tony Bland himself was the 96th victim when he died in 1993. As written the sentence counts Tony among the dead while saying he survived.

findings.claim: persistent vegetative state: “A condition where a patient can breathe independently but has no brain activity and no hope of recovery.”
findings.truth: A patient in a persistent vegetative state does have brain activity. The brainstem works, which is why they breathe and have sleep-wake cycles. What is lost is awareness of self and surroundings. “No brain activity” describes brain death, which is a different thing. The wrong definition sits twice: the data-def in content_html and glossary_terms[5].
findings.evidence: NHS / standard clinical definition of persistent vegetative state

findings.claim: Colossians 3:12 says: “Clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, gentleness and patience.”
findings.truth: NIV Colossians 3:12 reads “clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience”. “Humility” is missing from text given as a direct quotation.

findings.claim: Q2 is typed “1 mark - Give/Name” but reads “Give one reasons...” and its mark scheme says “1 marks for each valid reason, up to 2 marks”.
findings.truth: A theme question runs 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks, so the second question is worth 1 mark. The scheme must award one mark for one reason, and the stem must read “Give one reason”.

findings.claim: data-revision-tip: “Cover this box. Can you recall all 2 items listed here?”
findings.truth: The box lists four conditions for a legal abortion, not two.

findings.claim: data-revision-tip: “Cover this box. List the exam technique advice given here.”
findings.truth: The box holds the four types of euthanasia. It contains no exam technique, so the prompt asks for something that is not there.

findings.claim: As Dr Gunning warned: “Once you accept killing as a solution to a single problem ...”
findings.truth: The quotation is normally attributed to Dr Karel Gunning, a Dutch physician. “Dr Gunning” alone gives a student no usable source to name. The attribution is not wrong, only thin.

findings.claim: For AQA Religious Studies, you need to understand ...
findings.truth: Student-facing text must never name the exam board.

findings.claim: Q1 text is only “Which of the following best describes ‘barzakh’ in Islam?”. Options A-D sit inside the mark scheme.
findings.truth: A multiple-choice question whose options are hidden in the mark scheme cannot be answered. Every other lesson in the unit puts the options in the question text and the letter plus [1 mark] in the scheme.

findings.claim: Q2 is typed “1 mark - Give/Name” but reads “Give one Christian beliefs...” and its scheme says “Award one mark for each correct point, up to two marks”.
findings.truth: The second question in a theme is worth 1 mark. One belief, one mark.

findings.claim: Hindus, Buddhists, and Sikhs believe in reincarnation — being reborn in a new body after death.
findings.truth: Buddhism teaches rebirth, not reincarnation: no permanent soul or self passes into a new body (anatta). Grouping Buddhism with Hinduism and Sikhism states a known misconception as fact. The lesson’s own matching knowledge check labels reincarnation “Hinduism/Sikhism” only, so the page contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 Buddhism (anatta, dependent arising); raw/L05.txt knowledge_checks[4]

findings.claim: Christians and Muslims know they will be with God in heaven if they act the way he wants them to.
findings.truth: Neither tradition teaches certainty of heaven earned by conduct. Christians hold that judgement rests with God, and most Protestants teach salvation by grace through faith. Muslims hold that entry to Jannah depends on Allah’s judgement and mercy. “Know” overstates both.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.1 Christianity (salvation, grace); spec 3.1.2 Islam (Akhirah, judgement)

findings.claim: Three data-revision-tip prompts are broken fragments: “Recall the specific examples given for christians and Muslims believe in”, “Write down what you recall about muslims believe that after death”, “Write down what you recall about other religions have different views: Hindus”.
findings.truth: Generator output that never became a sentence. Students read these prompts, so they are rewritten as plain recall questions on the same content.

findings.claim: Q5 (12 marks) lists under “Points against”: “People from other religions (e.g. Hindus) believe in reincarnation, not heaven/hell - there is no agreement on what the afterlife looks like.”
findings.truth: Reincarnation is itself a belief in life after death, so the bullet supports the statement rather than opposing it. Two other “against” bullets are about disagreement inside Christianity, not about whether there is an afterlife. A student who used them would lose marks. This needs the indicative content rewriting, not a one-line patch, so it is left for Tom.

findings.claim: belief in akhirah (life after death) is one of the six articles of faith
findings.truth: The six articles are the Sunni formulation; Shi’a Islam sets out five roots of Usul ad-Din. The spec names both. Acceptable GCSE shorthand, so no edit.

findings.claim: All forms of euthanasia are currently illegal in the UK and treated as murder or manslaughter; and the September 2015 Commons vote of 118 for to 330 against.
findings.truth: Both verified correct as at 18 September 2026. Assisted suicide remains an offence under s.2 of the Suicide Act 1961; the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill has not become law and the Scottish bill fell at stage three on 17 March 2026. The 2015 vote was 330 against to 118 in favour on 11 September 2015. Re-check before the 2027 cohort.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Assisted suicide in the United Kingdom; Commons Library CBP-12181

summary: Five lessons checked. Lessons 4 and 5 are an older build and hold every hard error: the wrong abortion statute and jurisdiction, a Hillsborough death toll that counts Tony Bland among the dead while saying he survived, a persistent vegetative state defined as no brain activity, a truncated Colossians quotation, a multiple-choice question whose options were stored in its mark scheme, two 1-mark questions carrying 2-mark schemes, and Buddhism listed under reincarnation. Lesson 3 duplicates lesson 4 and needs Tom’s decision.
